analysis.one_liner: Requires farm equipment makers to sell repair parts, tools, software, and manuals to owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: The Agricultural Right to Repair Act never got a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee from September 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force manufacturers of tractors, combines, and other farm equipment to share the manuals, parts, diagnostic software, and repair tools they currently keep for themselves and their authorized dealers. Farmers and independent repair shops could then fix their own equipment instead of relying on the manufacturer's network. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and ranchers who own or lease equipment, and independent repair shops. They would get free access to manuals and diagnostic documentation, tools at no charge (owners) or at the best price any authorized dealer gets (shops), parts that cannot be locked to the manufacturer's approval, and the right to bypass digital locks to make repairs. This means faster and cheaper repairs, especially during planting and harvest when downtime is most costly.

how_it_helps.text: OEMs must make repair documentation, parts, software, firmware, and tools available to any equipment owner or independent repair provider on fair and reasonable terms, and must share equipment data with the owner or a repair provider the owner authorizes.

Documentation and repair tools would be free for equipment owners (only actual shipping costs allowed for physical copies), and independent shops would pay no more than the best price and get no worse terms than any authorized dealer.
Parts cannot be conditioned on manufacturer registration, pairing, or approval before they work, and shops cannot be required to become authorized dealers to use a part or tool.

The bill overrides the part of copyright law that otherwise makes bypassing digital locks illegal, allowing circumvention for diagnosing, maintaining, upgrading, or repairing farm equipment, for interoperability, and for security research.
Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission, and the FTC must write rules to carry the law out.
If a manufacturer stops offering a documentation item, part, software, or tool to its own authorized dealers, any copyright or patent the maker holds on it passes into the public domain.

analysis.who_pays: Farm equipment manufacturers and their authorized dealer networks. Manufacturers would lose the exclusive control over repair parts, software, and service revenue that comes from locking equipment to their own approval systems, and dealers would face competition from independent shops and do-it-yourself owners on parts and repair labor.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm equipment makers and dealer networks

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves limits in the name of safety and environmental law: it does not allow permanently disabling safety notification systems, making changes that put equipment out of compliance with safety or emissions rules, or any other illegal modification.

Manufacturers are not required to hand over trade secrets except as needed to supply repair material or processes on fair and reasonable terms, so some technical information could remain out of reach.

Makers of electronics-enabled machinery have argued that opening up firmware and diagnostic software creates risks of tampering, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and liability when non-factory repairs go wrong; the bill's carve-outs attempt to address this but would still be a major change to how these companies control their products.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and immediate: a farmer waiting on an authorized dealer during harvest loses time and money that independent repair access could save. The costs fall on manufacturers, who would give up a profitable service and parts business and would need to rework how they control equipment software. The bill tries to manage the real safety and emissions risks with explicit limits, though enforcing 'fair and reasonable terms' on proprietary software would inevitably produce disputes. On balance it is a well-aimed consumer and competition bill whose main weakness is the difficulty of policing compliance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee and then never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the bill in the House on September 20, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
Two days later, on September 22, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce.
Nine members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats; no Republican cosponsor is listed.
That was the last action of any kind: no subcommittee markup, no full committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate action ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers and their authorized dealer networks are better off, because they keep exclusive control over repair parts, diagnostic software, and service revenue, and farmers still must rely on that network.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm equipment makers and their dealers

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, routed it to the Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup, committee vote, or floor action for it in the 15 months before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support or opposition vote is on the record — the bill never advanced far enough to force one.

industries.note: The bill would end their exclusive control over the manuals, parts, diagnostic software, and unlocking tools for the tractors and combines they sell, cutting into service and parts revenue and forbidding software locks that require manufacturer approval before a part works.
Dealers would lose the near-monopoly on farm equipment repair, since owners and independent shops could get the same parts and tools at the same prices and terms dealers get.
They would gain legal access to documentation, tools at dealer-equivalent prices, and parts that work without manufacturer pairing, letting them compete for repair work.
Farmers could fix their own equipment or use any shop, with free manuals and tools, reducing downtime and repair costs during critical planting and harvest windows.
